headline: Apollo's Daily-Pricing Pledge Is Also a Confession
lede: Apollo Global Management, the world's largest private credit manager, announced on its May 6 first-quarter earnings call that it will value its entire $830 billion credit book at daily estimated prices by the end of September 2026. Jeffrey Gundlach, the bond investor and DoubleLine Capital founder, noted the unspoken corollary: a pledge to start doing it later is an admission it is not being done now.
body:
Apollo Global Management (APO), with more than a trillion dollars in total assets under management and $830 billion in credit alone, set two deadlines on May 6: corporate investment-grade fixed income to be daily-priced by June 30, direct lending and asset-backed finance by September 30. Chief executive Marc Rowan framed the commitment as an industry leadership move. It landed the same day the Financial Stability Board published a report warning that the private credit market — which it estimates at $1.5 to $2.0 trillion globally — “has not been tested during a severe economic downturn.”

The issue goes to the structural DNA of *private credit* — loans made outside the public bond market, negotiated bilaterally, designed to be held to maturity rather than traded. Because there is no exchange where these instruments change hands, no continuous observable price exists. Managers have historically relied on *mark-to-model* methods: internal discounted-cash-flow assumptions, supplemented by third-party appraisal firms, updated quarterly. Critics call this approach “mark-to-myth” — prices are held at par until a borrower defaults, with no gradual market discovery in between. The gap is not merely theoretical. Data from iCapital, a private wealth platform, shows three different lenders simultaneously valuing loans to the same software company at 91, 82, and 77 cents on the dollar — a 14-percentage-point spread, with one treating the position as distressed while another marked it near par.

Apollo’s announcement was not unprovoked. In the first quarter of 2026, the firm’s approximately $25 billion Apollo Debt Solutions *BDC* — a Business Development Company, a regulated vehicle sold to wealthy individuals with limited quarterly withdrawal windows — received redemption requests amounting to 11.2 percent of shares outstanding against a 5 percent contractual cap. Apollo honored roughly $730 million of the $1.5 billion demanded, about 45 cents on the dollar of investor requests. The episode exposed a structural tension at the heart of semi-liquid private credit products: the underlying loans are illiquid and priced quarterly, yet the fund wrapper promises near-daily *NAV* (net asset value) figures and periodic liquidity. Ares Management (ARES) gated its own non-traded BDC in the same period.

Gundlach has been building toward this reading for over a year. In June 2025 he invoked the period before the 2008 financial crisis — “feels like 2006” was his formulation — warning that private credit repackaged into retail-accessible wrappers resembles the subprime mortgage packaging that preceded it. His specific charge: these loans are effectively priced at only two values, par until the moment of default, with no gradual market signal in between. He cited the case of Renovo, a home-renovation company whose private credit lenders held its debt at par weeks before it filed for bankruptcy with liabilities of $100 million to $500 million against assets under $50,000. On the day of Apollo’s earnings call, Bloomberg ran a separate headline: “Gundlach Warns Investors Will Lose Money on Private Credit Funds.” His commentary on the Apollo announcement was terse: the pledge is a confession, not a transparency upgrade.

Rowan explicitly acknowledged that some peers are “resisting this transparency,” positioning Apollo as an industry leader while creating implicit pressure on Ares and other large private credit managers. The regulatory weather is shifting regardless. Fitch Ratings reported a private credit default rate of 5.8 percent in early 2026, the highest in years, while publicly traded BDCs fell roughly 13 percent on the S&P BDC Index in 2025 even as private equivalents reported gains of 8 to 10 percent — a gap that signals either deteriorating underlying quality or stale marks flattering private fund returns. The *FSB* report, SEC scrutiny of redemption-gate mechanisms, and Congressional attention to private fund disclosures all point toward mandatory more-frequent valuation requirements. Apollo is moving first, presumably to shape the standard.

concepts.definition: Loans made directly from a fund to a corporate borrower, outside the public bond market. Because these instruments are not exchange-traded, they have no continuous observable market price and are valued periodically using internal models or third-party appraisers. The asset class has grown to roughly $1.5–2.0 trillion globally.

A valuation method in which an illiquid asset is priced not by an observed market transaction but by a financial model — typically a discounted cash flow calculation using the manager’s own assumptions about discount rates, credit risk, and recovery. The alternative, mark-to-market, uses actual prices from recent comparable trades.

A pejorative phrase used by critics of private credit arguing that fund valuations are essentially fictional — optimistic internal models that hold loans at par until a forced write-down, obscuring true credit deterioration and smoothing reported returns. A play on the accounting term “mark-to-market.”

A regulated investment vehicle under the U.S. Investment Company Act of 1940 that pools capital to lend to or invest in mid-sized private companies. Non-traded BDCs are sold to accredited individual investors and offer limited periodic redemptions — typically 5 percent of NAV per quarter — rather than daily liquidity.

The per-share value of a fund, calculated as total assets minus liabilities divided by shares outstanding. For private funds holding illiquid loans, NAV is estimated rather than derived from market prices, and the frequency and rigor of that estimation is the central controversy the Apollo announcement addresses.

A contractual mechanism in a private fund that limits how much capital investors can withdraw in any given period — typically a percentage of the fund’s net asset value per quarter. Gates prevent a run on illiquid assets but can strand investors who urgently need liquidity, as happened with Apollo’s ADS BDC in Q1 2026.

A private fund structure — including interval funds and non-traded BDCs — that offers periodic but limited redemption windows, more liquid than a locked closed-end fund but far less so than a mutual fund or ETF. The mismatch between daily NAV pricing and infrequent actual liquidity is the structural tension at the center of this debate.

An international body established after the 2008 financial crisis that monitors and makes recommendations about global financial system vulnerabilities. Its reports carry significant weight with national regulators but are advisory rather than legally binding. The FSB published a dedicated private credit vulnerabilities report on May 6, 2026.

fact_check: The tweet describes the commitment as “by year-end,” but Apollo’s May 6 earnings call gave a more aggressive and specific timeline: corporate investment-grade fixed income by June 30, 2026, and direct lending and asset-backed finance by September 30, 2026 — the end of Q3, not calendar year-end. The earlier Bloomberg report from March 2026 used looser “year-end” framing, so the tweet may reflect that initial characterization rather than Rowan’s firmer Q3 commitment.
